questions.question: A Pakistani online game publisher's account-takeover model shows input drift within tolerance, yet confirmed takeovers it missed have tripled since attackers changed tactics. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Tighten the input drift thresholds so alerts fire sooner
options.B: Lower the takeover alert threshold so the model flags more logins
options.C: Monitor detection rates against verified takeover outcomes
options.D: Keep uptime and response time as the takeover model's main indicators

questions.key_concept: Concept drift changes the link between inputs and outcomes, which input metrics can miss; monitoring against real outcomes, such as confirmed missed takeovers, reveals it.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the indicator in place could change at all if the meaning of the inputs changed.
questions.correct_explanation: Attackers changed tactics, so the link between inputs and takeovers shifted while the inputs themselves look much the same: concept drift. Input drift metrics cannot see that, which is why they stay green while missed takeovers triple. Tracking detection against verified takeover outcomes, with thresholds that trigger review, shows decay directly. Tighter input thresholds only make the same blind measure more sensitive; they would still miss a change in meaning.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because sensitive alerts catch drift sooner. But the inputs have not shifted much; the change is in what they mean, which input metrics cannot measure.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because flagging more seems to catch more takeovers. But a model that never learned the new tactics may still score them low, while false alerts rise.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because availability is easy to measure. But a model can run perfectly while missing takeovers; uptime says nothing about decision quality.

tips: Eliminate: B lowers the alert threshold, but a model that never learned the new tactics may still score them low, and D tracks availability, which says nothing about decision quality.
Final two: C beats A because concept drift shows most directly in outcomes; tighter input thresholds sharpen a measure that cannot see changes in meaning.
Exam cue: inputs steady but results worse points to concept drift; recommend monitoring against real outcomes, not just input distributions.

questions.question: A French city's AI traffic-signal model is measured only on its travel-time target, which it meets, but residents report pedestrian waits near a care home have doubled. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Keep the approved travel-time target as the model's main measure
options.B: Have the model owner assess and monitor impacts on pedestrians
options.C: Retrain the model now so that pedestrian waiting times weigh more heavily
options.D: Recheck travel-time accuracy on a fresh sample of junctions

questions.key_concept: Monitoring covers a system's impacts on people, not just its target metric; owners set impact indicators and thresholds within approved tolerances before tuning.
questions.pre_read: Ask who bears the cost of what the model optimizes, and whether anyone measures it.
questions.correct_explanation: The model optimizes travel time, and its effect on people crossing near the care home is not measured. The model owner needs to assess that effect and monitor impact indicators, such as pedestrian waits at sensitive crossings, with thresholds inside approved tolerances. Retraining to weigh pedestrian waits may be the owner's eventual fix, but it is a design choice, and without those indicators nobody can show it worked or spot the next side effect.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the model meets its approved target. But a target on travel time says nothing about harm to pedestrians, which nobody measures.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it addresses the complaint directly. But without impact indicators nobody can show the fix worked or spot new side effects, and retraining is a change.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because fresh data checks accuracy. But the model's travel-time accuracy is not in doubt; its effects on pedestrians are what go unmeasured.

tips: Eliminate: A treats meeting the target as enough, though targets omit side effects, and D rechecks travel-time accuracy, which is not in question.
Final two: B beats C because the harm must be measured before a retrain can be judged; tuning first fixes one symptom without a measure.
Exam cue: supervise impacts on people, not just the metric a model optimizes; expect indicators and thresholds for the groups it affects.

questions.question: A Swiss city's school-placement model, retrained each spring, assigns children to schools; families can appeal, but its decision log keeps only each child's final placement. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Log each placement's inputs and model version with the outcome
options.B: Have staff rerun disputed cases through the current model version
options.C: Publish how the placement model weighs each input
options.D: Keep the placement log longer so appeals can be answered

questions.key_concept: A decision log must hold each decision's inputs and model version, so a contested outcome can be explained and reviewed.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a reviewer would need to see to explain one family's placement months later.
questions.correct_explanation: An appeal needs what the model was given and which version decided; a log of outcomes alone can explain neither. Logging inputs and model version with each placement makes every decision traceable. Rerunning disputed cases through the current version sounds like reperformance, but without the original inputs staff may not rerun the same case, and a since-retrained model shows today's answer, not why the original placement was made.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because rerunning looks like reperformance. But without the original inputs the case may differ, and a changed model gives today's answer, not the original reason.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because transparency helps families understand. But a general description of weights cannot explain or correct one child's placement.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because longer retention supports appeals. But keeping outcome-only records longer adds nothing about why each placement was made.

tips: Eliminate: C explains the model in general, not one child's placement, and D keeps the same outcome-only records longer, which adds no explanation.
Final two: A beats B because logged inputs and version let reviewers trace the actual decision; rerunning today's model may use different inputs and a different model.
Exam cue: for contestable AI decisions, a log needs inputs, model version, output and final action; outcomes alone cannot support an appeal.

questions.question: A Tanzanian health ministry will launch a generative AI assistant answering pregnancy questions by text message. Which acceptance criterion should the IS auditor consider MOST important?

options.A: Share of sampled answers that pilot users rate as helpful
options.B: Average response time of under two seconds per text message
options.C: Accuracy on the vendor's standard medical question-answer benchmark
options.D: Cap on unsafe or invented advice in clinician-reviewed tests

questions.key_concept: Acceptance criteria for generative AI include a limit on confabulated or unsafe answers, set before testing and judged by qualified reviewers.
questions.pre_read: Ask who could tell a fluent wrong answer from a right one, and whether the criterion relies on them.
questions.correct_explanation: A pregnancy assistant's worst failures are confident answers that are false, known as confabulation, or advice that is unsafe. Only clinicians reviewing realistic scenarios can catch them, so the key criterion is a cap on such answers, set before testing. Users' helpfulness ratings matter, but users cannot judge medical accuracy, and a confident wrong answer often feels most helpful.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because user acceptance matters. But pilot users cannot tell accurate medical advice from confident invention, so high ratings can coexist with harmful answers.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because speed affects usability. But a fast answer can still be wrong; response time measures service, not the safety of the advice.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because benchmarks look objective. But a vendor benchmark uses other questions and settings, not pregnancy questions asked by text in this context.

tips: Eliminate: B measures speed, not whether the advice is safe, and C relies on a vendor benchmark built from other questions and settings.
Final two: D beats A because clinicians can spot confident but wrong advice; users rate how helpful an answer feels, not whether it is medically right.
Exam cue: for generative AI giving advice, expect a pre-set limit on confabulated or unsafe answers, judged by qualified reviewers on realistic scenarios.

questions.question: In validation, a Belgian student-loan fund's model approved the same share of Dutch- and French-speaking applicants, but wrongly declined creditworthy French speakers three times as often. What is the IS auditor's BEST conclusion?

options.A: Equal approval shares show the model treats both language groups fairly
options.B: One fairness measure is met while error rates show unequal harm
options.C: Removing language from the inputs would make the model fair
options.D: The model has drifted since its training data was collected

questions.key_concept: Fairness measures can conflict: equal approval rates can coexist with unequal error rates, so owners must choose and justify the measures used.
questions.pre_read: Ask which fairness measure the claim rests on, and what a different measure shows.
questions.correct_explanation: Equal approval shares satisfy one fairness measure, but creditworthy French speakers are wrongly declined three times as often, so the harm of errors falls unequally. Fairness measures can conflict; the model owner, with legal input, must choose which apply and justify the choice, and the IS auditor reports this unequal harm. Treating equal approval shares as proof of fairness reads one measure as the whole picture.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because equal outcomes look fair. But equal approval shares can mask unequal errors; here creditworthy French speakers are wrongly declined three times as often.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because dropping the attribute seems neutral. But other inputs, such as home province or university, can act as proxies, and only outcome testing shows remaining bias.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because drift is a common AI risk. But these are validation results, before deployment; nothing here shows change over time.

tips: Eliminate: C drops language from the inputs, though proxies can carry the same bias, and D claims drift from validation results, which show no change over time.
Final two: B beats A because fairness measures can conflict; equal approval shares do not show that errors fall evenly across groups.
Exam cue: when a fairness claim rests on one measure, check error rates by group too; the model owner must justify which measures apply.

questions.question: An Ecuadorian flower exporter's pricing assistant can change list prices through a connected tool; its red team tested only the underlying model, with no tool attached. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Add an output filter that blocks harmful replies to staff
options.B: Rerun the same red-team tests after each assistant update
options.C: Ask the vendor for its red-team report on the base model
options.D: Widen the red team's scope to the assistant as it is deployed

questions.key_concept: Red teaming covers the system as deployed, with its tools and permissions; a model-only test cannot show what a manipulated system could do.
questions.pre_read: List what the deployed system can do, then compare it with what the red team actually exercised.
questions.correct_explanation: The red team tested a model that could not act, so nobody knows what a manipulated or mistaken assistant could do to list prices, which is where the harm lies. Red teaming must cover the system as deployed, with its tools, permissions and data sources. Repeating the model-only tests after each update is sound regression practice, but it keeps the same blind spot and never exercises the price changes.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because filters catch harmful text. But a manipulated assistant can change prices without any harmful reply, so a reply filter misses the real harm.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because retesting after updates is good practice. But it repeats the same model-only scope and never tests what the assistant can do to prices.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the vendor tested the base model. But that testing cannot cover this assistant's own tool, permissions or pricing context.

tips: Eliminate: A filters replies, though a manipulated assistant can change prices without a harmful reply, and C relies on vendor tests of the base model, not this setup.
Final two: D beats B because the untested risk is what the deployed assistant can do to prices; repeating model-only tests keeps the same blind spot.
Exam cue: red-team the AI system as deployed, with its tools, data sources and permissions; a model-only test cannot show what the system can actually do.

questions.question: An Icelandic avalanche-warning service validated its risk model on complete sensor records, but storms often freeze or cut sensors. Which test should the IS auditor recommend as MOST important before go-live?

options.A: Revalidation by an independent team on the same sensor records
options.B: Robustness testing on degraded and missing sensor readings
options.C: A backtest on past storm seasons with sensor gaps filled in
options.D: A load test of the warning website and text alerts during storms

questions.key_concept: Robustness testing feeds a model the degraded inputs it will meet in use, such as missing or frozen readings, before it is relied on.
questions.pre_read: Compare the conditions in the validation data with the conditions on the day the model matters most.
questions.correct_explanation: Validation used complete records, yet storms, when warnings matter most, bring frozen and missing readings the model never saw. Robustness testing with such inputs shows whether it still warns sensibly or fails safely. A backtest on past storm seasons looks closer, but with the gaps filled in it again feeds clean inputs, so nobody learns how the model behaves when sensors fail.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because independence strengthens validation. But validators using the same complete records never see frozen or missing readings, so the blind spot remains.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it covers storm seasons. But with the gaps filled in, the model again gets clean inputs and never meets the frozen or missing readings it will get live.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because storms bring traffic spikes. But a load test checks the website and alerts, not whether the model's warnings hold up when readings go missing.

tips: Eliminate: A has independent validators reuse the same complete records, so the blind spot remains, and D tests website capacity, not the model's behavior on bad inputs.
Final two: B beats C because a storm backtest with the gaps filled in still feeds clean inputs; only degraded and missing readings show behavior when sensors fail.
Exam cue: when inputs in use will be noisier or patchier than in validation, expect robustness testing on those inputs before go-live.

questions.question: A Portuguese cork producer's engineers downloaded a popular pre-trained vision model from a public hub and plan to run it on plant servers for a sorting pilot. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Rely on the model's popularity on the hub as evidence of safety
options.B: Test the model's accuracy on the plant's own cork images
options.C: Verify the model's source and integrity before relying on it
options.D: Add stricter firewall rules around the plant's servers

questions.key_concept: Downloaded models, like other supply-chain components, are untrusted until their source and integrity are verified; model files can carry hidden behavior or code.
questions.pre_read: Ask how the team knows the file it loaded is the one its publisher released, and what it contains.
questions.correct_explanation: A model file from a public hub is a supply-chain component: it may be tampered with, carry a hidden backdoor or, in some file formats, run code when loaded. Treating it as untrusted until its source and integrity are verified, for example against a publisher's hash, comes first. Testing accuracy on the plant's images shows fitness, but a backdoored model can score well while its trigger stays dormant.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because popular models seem well vetted. But downloads are not checks; attackers target popular models, and popularity says nothing about this file's integrity.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because fitness testing is needed anyway. But a tampered model can score well on normal images while carrying a trigger or malicious code.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because firewalls protect servers. But the model came in through an allowed download and runs inside the network; a firewall cannot inspect it.

tips: Eliminate: A takes popularity as proof of safety, which no download count gives, and D adds perimeter rules, though the file arrived through an allowed path.
Final two: C beats B because integrity must be established before relying on any test result; a backdoored model can pass accuracy tests.
Exam cue: treat downloaded models, datasets and libraries as untrusted supply-chain components until their source and integrity are verified.
questions.framework_ref: MITRE ATLAS AML.T0010 (AI Supply Chain Compromise); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SI-7 (Software, Firmware, and Information Integrity)

questions.question: A Lithuanian fertility clinic plans to publish its trained treatment-outcome model, built from patient records, so researchers can download and use it freely. Which threat should the IS auditor consider MOST significant?

options.A: Researchers rebuilding a working copy of the model from its outputs
options.B: Attackers learning whether a patient's records were used in training
options.C: Researchers using the model on patient records beyond its intended use
options.D: Attackers poisoning the clinic's model by retraining their own copies

questions.key_concept: A released model can leak its training data: membership inference reveals who was in it, which for sensitive data is itself a disclosure.
questions.pre_read: Ask what someone holding the model could learn about the people whose records trained it.
questions.correct_explanation: Once released, the model can be queried without limit, and membership inference can reveal whether a person's records helped train it. Being in a fertility clinic's training data discloses treatment, a serious, irreversible privacy harm. Misuse beyond the intended use is a real concern too, but usage terms and a model card can narrow it, while leaked membership cannot be undone once the model is out.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because extraction is a real AI threat. But the clinic is publishing the model itself; there is nothing left to steal by copying it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because released models get misused. But usage terms and a model card can narrow misuse, while leaked patient membership cannot be taken back.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because poisoning is a major AI threat. But retraining a downloaded copy changes only that copy, not the clinic's own model.

tips: Eliminate: A worries about copying a model that is being published anyway, and D assumes changing a downloaded copy alters the clinic's own model.
Final two: B beats C because revealing who was in a fertility dataset discloses treatment and cannot be undone; misuse can be narrowed by terms and documentation.
Exam cue: before releasing a model trained on sensitive personal data, weigh membership inference and data reconstruction; the model itself can leak who was in it.

questions.question: A Hungarian bike-sharing firm's support chatbot has its rental-database password written into its system prompt; staff say riders cannot see the prompt. Which risk should the IS auditor consider GREATEST?

options.A: Attackers breaching the chatbot's firewall to read the stored prompt
options.B: The vendor logging prompt text, including the password
options.C: Riders losing rental lookups after the password is changed
options.D: Riders prompting the chatbot into revealing the password

questions.key_concept: System prompts can be extracted by prompting, so they are not a safe place for secrets; anything in them may reach any user.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether 'cannot see' means 'cannot obtain' when users can talk to the system.
questions.correct_explanation: Any rider can chat with the bot, and system prompts can often be extracted by asking cleverly, a known direct prompting attack. A password in the prompt is therefore exposed to every rider who chats, and any of them could turn it against the rental database. Vendor logging of prompts would be an exposure too, but to one known party, not to every rider.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because breaches expose stored data. But extraction needs no breach; riders reach the prompt's contents through the normal chat window.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because vendors may keep prompt logs. But that exposes the password to one known party; extraction exposes it to every rider who chats.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because rotating credentials can break integrations. But lost lookups are an operational nuisance, not the exposure of a database password to the public.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes a firewall breach, though extraction works through the normal chat, and C is an operational nuisance, not an exposure.
Final two: D beats B because extraction opens the password to every rider who chats; vendor logs expose it to one known party.
Exam cue: treat system prompts as readable by users; secrets in a prompt are exposed, whatever staff believe users can see.

questions.question: A Scottish distillery's AI procurement agent reads emailed invoices into its chat and pays each one once any message in that chat shows a manager's approval. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the agent match each invoice to its purchase order first
options.B: Cap each agent payment at a small amount to limit losses
options.C: Have a finance manager review the agent's recorded approvals monthly
options.D: Enforce manager approval within the payment system itself

questions.key_concept: Human approval for high-impact agent actions must be enforced outside the model; an approval that exists only in the agent's chat can be faked.
questions.pre_read: Ask who, or what, could produce the record that says a manager approved.
questions.correct_explanation: Approval exists only in the agent's chat, and the agent reads untrusted invoices into that same chat, so injected invoice text can fake an approval. Enforcing approval in the payment system, where a manager must act and the agent cannot, makes the control hold whatever the agent is told. Capping each payment reduces the cost of each error, but a manipulated agent could still pay many invoices with no real approval.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because matching invoices to orders is a sound payment control. But the agent runs the match itself, so injected invoice text can still steer it, and no manager approves.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a cap limits each loss. But a manipulated agent could still pay many capped invoices, each on an approval faked by injected text in its chat.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because review catches problems. But monthly review comes after payment, and the chat approvals it checks may have been faked by invoice text.

tips: Eliminate: A has the agent check its own work, which injected invoice text can steer, and C reviews chat approvals, which invoice text may have faked, only after payment.
Final two: D beats B because approval enforced outside the agent stops unapproved payments; a cap only limits each one while faked chat approvals continue.
Exam cue: when an agent needs a high-impact power, put the approval where the agent can neither grant nor record it; when it never needs the power, remove it.

questions.question: A Croatian disability-benefits office's model that sets home-care hours has exceeded its error tolerance for three weeks; the data team logged it as a backlog item. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Treat it as an AI incident and triage by impact on people
options.B: Schedule retraining for the next quarterly model release
options.C: Escalate it to the security team as a possible breach
options.D: Have the data team find the root cause before acting

questions.key_concept: Performance beyond tolerance in a decision about people is an AI incident, triaged by impact, not a backlog item or a security matter.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether people are being affected right now, and which process is built to respond to that.
questions.correct_explanation: Errors beyond tolerance in a model that sets care hours for people with disabilities are likely affecting their care now, which makes this an AI incident, not routine maintenance. Raising it as an incident and triaging by impact on people decides how fast to contain it, for example by reviewing affected cases or disengaging the model. Root cause analysis is needed, but leading with it leaves wrong care hours in place meanwhile.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because retraining through a release is controlled. But it leaves wrong care hours in place for months and skips triage and containment.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because incidents are often security events. But nothing suggests an attack; AI incidents include harmful outputs and tolerance breaches without any breach.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because root cause matters. But diagnosis comes after the incident is raised and triaged; meanwhile people keep receiving wrong care hours.

tips: Eliminate: B queues the fault for a routine release while people are affected, and C routes it as a security breach, though nothing points to an attack.
Final two: A beats D because raising and triaging the incident sets how fast harm is contained; root cause analysis follows, it does not lead.
Exam cue: a tolerance breach in a model that decides about people is an AI incident; raise it, triage by impact on people, then investigate.

questions.question: A South African emergency dispatch center receives four AI incident reports in one morning. Which should the IS auditor expect incident managers to triage FIRST?

options.A: Priority model's error rate on minority-language calls above tolerance
options.B: Website chatbot jailbroken, its insulting replies shared widely online
options.C: Rota-planning model proposing uneven weekend shifts for night dispatchers
options.D: Transcription dashboard down for an hour, with calls still handled

questions.key_concept: Triage ranks AI incidents by likely harm to people, then the business; a quiet tolerance breach in a live model can outrank a visible attack.
questions.pre_read: For each report, ask who is being harmed now, how badly and how many.
questions.correct_explanation: An error rate above tolerance in the call-priority model means some minority-language emergency calls are ranked too low right now, which can delay help to people in danger; it ranks highest on likelihood and impact. The jailbroken chatbot needs follow-up as a security and AI incident, but its harm is reputational and puts no one in danger; a visible attack is not automatically the top priority.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a public, successful attack feels most urgent. But its harm is reputational, while misranked emergency calls can endanger lives now.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because fairness to staff matters. But uneven rotas are an internal planning issue a person can correct, with no immediate harm to callers.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because outages are classic incidents. But calls were still handled during the hour, so the impact on callers was small and has ended.

tips: Eliminate: C is an internal planning issue with no immediate harm, and D was a short outage during which calls were still handled.
Final two: A beats B because a tolerance breach in a live emergency model harms callers now; the jailbreak's harm is reputational.
Exam cue: triage AI incidents by likelihood and impact on people; a tolerance breach in a live model can outrank a visible attack.

questions.question: After a Peruvian blood bank switched off its generative AI chatbot for showing donors others' appointment details, the privacy officer wants every chat log deleted at once. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Delete the logs now to limit further exposure of donors' data
options.B: Keep the model version and settings, and delete the chat logs
options.C: Keep the logs under restricted access until the investigation ends
options.D: Have the vendor retrain the chatbot on corrected data straight away

questions.key_concept: Incident chat logs are evidence that a generative rerun cannot replace: keep them under restricted access for the investigation, then dispose on schedule.
questions.pre_read: Ask what investigators and affected people will need from these records before deciding to destroy them.
questions.correct_explanation: Generative answers cannot be reliably reproduced later, so the chat logs are the best record of what the chatbot said and whose details it exposed. Deleting them destroys the evidence for root cause, notification and any regulator's questions; restricted access protects donors meanwhile. Keeping the model version and settings looks thorough, but a rerun may never repeat what donors actually saw.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because deletion feels protective. But the chatbot is already off, and deleting logs destroys the evidence needed to find the cause and confirm who was affected.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because version and settings let the chatbot be rerun. But generative answers vary between runs, so only the logs show what donors actually saw.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the vendor can fix the model. But retraining before the cause is known changes the system under investigation and may not fix the fault.

tips: Eliminate: A destroys evidence the investigation needs, though the chatbot is already off, and D changes the system before anyone knows the cause.
Final two: C beats B because only the logs show what the chatbot actually exposed; version and settings make a rerun possible, not a faithful replay.
Exam cue: generative answers cannot be reliably regenerated, so incident logs are primary evidence; restrict access, investigate, then dispose of them on schedule.

questions.question: A Costa Rican park service's chatbot told hikers a closed trail was open; the problem record names 'model hallucination' as root cause and is closed. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Reopen the problem and find why the chatbot gave that answer
options.B: Add a notice that the chatbot's answers may be inaccurate
options.C: Switch to a larger model that hallucinates less often
options.D: Keep the problem closed and note hallucination as a known limit

questions.key_concept: 'Hallucination' names a symptom, not a cause; problem management traces it to data, retrieval, prompt or integration before closing.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the recorded cause would tell anyone what to change so it does not happen again.
questions.correct_explanation: Hallucination, which NIST calls confabulation, describes what the chatbot did, not why. The cause may be a trail-status source that was never updated, retrieval of an old notice or a prompt gap, and each needs a different fix. The problem stays open until that cause is found and a fix verified. A warning notice is a fair extra safeguard, but hikers would still be sent onto closed trails.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because generative AI can be wrong. But a disclaimer leaves the cause in place, and hikers relying on the chatbot would still be sent onto closed trails.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because larger models can be more accurate. But if the trail data or retrieval is the cause, a new model repeats the error; the cause is unknown.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because confabulation is a known limit. But a known limit is a symptom; problem management still needs the specific cause and a verified fix.

tips: Eliminate: C swaps the model before the cause is known, and D accepts a label for the symptom as if it were a root cause.
Final two: A beats B because finding the cause lets it be fixed; a disclaimer leaves hikers exposed to the same wrong answer.
Exam cue: 'the model hallucinated' is like 'operator error': a symptom; expect root cause in data, retrieval, prompt or integration before a problem closes.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Boatyard safety manual
questions.question: A Fijian boatyard's staff assistant uses retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over a folder holding three versions of its safety manual, none marked current. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Retrain the assistant's model on the text of the latest manual
options.B: Tell the assistant in its prompt to prefer the newest manual
options.C: Have a named owner keep only the approved manual in the index
options.D: Have staff check each safety answer against the printed manual

questions.key_concept: Documents used for retrieval are AI data: each needs a named owner who keeps only approved, current versions in the index.
questions.pre_read: Ask where the assistant's answers come from at run time, and who decides what is in that source.
questions.correct_explanation: Retrieval answers from whatever sits in the index, so three unmarked versions mean staff may get superseded safety rules. A named owner who keeps only the approved manual indexed fixes the source and makes someone accountable for it. A prompt telling the assistant to prefer the newest version is weaker: nothing marks which file is newest, and a prompt instruction guides the model but does not control its sources.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because training seems to teach the right rules. But a RAG assistant answers from retrieved files at run time; retraining leaves the old manuals in the index.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it is quick. But no file is marked current, and a prompt only guides the model; it cannot control which documents are retrieved.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because people catch errors. But it pushes the control onto every reader after answers are given and leaves wrong safety rules in circulation.

tips: Eliminate: A retrains a model that reads its sources at answer time, and D moves the control to every reader after answers are given.
Final two: C beats B because an owner controlling the indexed content fixes the source; a prompt instruction guides the model but controls nothing.
Exam cue: for RAG, the retrieved documents are data; like any training set, they need an owner, approval and current versions.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Training file sources
questions.question: A Moldovan winery retrains its harvest-timing model weekly on sensor files that any of its 40 vineyard contractors can upload to a shared cloud folder. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Compare each retrained model's accuracy with the previous version's
options.B: Encrypt the shared folder so outsiders cannot read the files
options.C: Validate each file's source, integrity and values before training
options.D: Retrain monthly so that fewer contractor files reach the model

questions.key_concept: Training data is a control point: files from unverified sources can change model behavior, so pipelines check each input's source, integrity and values.
questions.pre_read: Ask who can put records into the training data, and what checks them before the model learns from them.
questions.correct_explanation: Whatever lands in the folder becomes training data, so one careless or malicious contractor can change what the model learns without touching any code. Verifying each file's source and integrity, for example files hashed at the sensor, and checking values against expected ranges, catches many tampered or careless records before training. Comparing accuracy after retraining comes too late and can miss targeted tampering that skews particular vineyards or dates.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a drop in accuracy can reveal bad data. But it acts after training, and targeted tampering can skew some vineyards while overall accuracy holds.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because encryption protects data. But it protects confidentiality; anyone allowed to upload can still add or alter training files.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because fewer retraining runs mean fewer chances. But each run still takes in unverified files; frequency does not control what enters the data.

tips: Eliminate: B protects confidentiality, not what may be added, and D retrains less often but still learns from unverified files.
Final two: C beats A because checking source, integrity and values before training stops many bad records; accuracy checks afterward can miss targeted changes.
Exam cue: when many parties can feed a model's training data, look for source and integrity controls before training, not only checks after it.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Model-made labels
questions.question: An Ethiopian teff cooperative is training a new grain-quality model on 50,000 grades assigned automatically by the older model it will replace. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Have the owner check a sample of the grades against expert graders
options.B: Add more grades from the older model so that errors average out
options.C: Train the model now and judge it on its test set accuracy
options.D: Treat the older model's past audit as proof its grades are right

questions.key_concept: Labels produced by another model carry its errors into training and testing; check them against expert judgment before relying on them.
questions.pre_read: Ask who or what decided the right answers the new model will learn from.
questions.correct_explanation: Labels produced by the model being replaced carry its errors, so the new model will learn them, and a test set graded the same way will reward copying them. Checking a sample of the automatic grades against expert graders shows how reliable the labels are, and whether they need correcting, before training. Judging the model on test accuracy misleads: it measures agreement with the old model, not correct grading.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because more data often helps. But more grades from the same model repeat its errors; volume does not make labels correct.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because testing is the usual check. But the test labels come from the old model too, so accuracy measures agreement with it, not correctness.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the old model was reviewed. But a past audit of a system is not evidence that each of its 50,000 grades is right for training.

tips: Eliminate: B adds more labels carrying the same errors, and D treats a past audit as proof that every grade is correct.
Final two: A beats C because the test labels share the old model's errors; checking labels against experts first gives the model, and its test, reliable answers.
Exam cue: when labels come from another model, its errors become ground truth; check them against people who know the answer before training.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Outcome definitions
questions.question: A Lebanese hospital group changed its definition of a readmission from 30 to 14 days last year and retrains its readmission model on records labeled under both rules. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Older records may describe patient behavior that has since changed
options.B: The model learns two different meanings of one outcome
options.C: The board did not approve the new readmission definition
options.D: The retrained model will predict fewer readmissions than before

questions.key_concept: Labels must mean the same thing across the training data; a changed outcome definition requires relabeling or separating older records.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the model is taught to predict, and whether that meant the same thing in every year of data.
questions.correct_explanation: A 30-day readmission and a 14-day readmission are different outcomes, so records labeled under both rules teach the model inconsistent answers: similar patients count as readmitted in one year and not the next. Its predictions match neither definition cleanly, and relabeling older records to one rule is the fix. Older data drifting from current behavior is a real general concern, but here the labels themselves conflict.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because old data can go stale. But the stated problem is that the label's meaning changed, which corrupts training even if behavior did not.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because definitions matter. But setting a clinical outcome definition is management's call; the board approves risk appetite, not label rules.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because predictions will shift. But fewer predicted readmissions under a stricter rule is expected; the concern is the mixed labels, not the direction.

tips: Eliminate: C sends a clinical definition to the board, which approves appetite, not labels, and D describes the expected effect of a stricter rule.
Final two: B beats A because a changed label definition corrupts the training answers themselves; general staleness is a weaker, separate concern.
Exam cue: when what counts as the outcome changes, check that every training record is labeled under one consistent definition.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Bill-default testing
questions.question: A Kuwaiti electricity retailer tested its bill-default model on a random 20% of three years of accounts, drawn from every month. Which additional test should the IS auditor request FIRST?

options.A: A fresh random 20% sample from the same three years of accounts
options.B: Five-fold cross-validation using random folds across the three years
options.C: A comparison of the model's results with last year's model
options.D: A test on the latest months, held back entirely from training

questions.key_concept: Models that predict future events need out-of-time testing on the latest period; random splits across time leak later information into training.
questions.pre_read: Ask when the test records happened compared with the training records, not only how they were picked.
questions.correct_explanation: A random split mixes every month into both training and testing, so the model is tested on periods it already learned from, including months later than many of its training records. An out-of-time test, holding back the most recent months, shows how the model performs on data from after training, as it will in use. Random cross-validation looks more rigorous but repeats the same mixing across five folds.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a fresh sample feels independent. But it is drawn the same way, so it repeats the time mixing that inflates the score.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because cross-validation is a recognized technique. But random folds still mix earlier and later months, so every fold shares the same flaw.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a comparison gives context. But beating last year's model on mixed data says nothing about performance on future accounts.

tips: Eliminate: A redraws the same kind of random sample, and C compares models without testing either on later data.
Final two: D beats B because only holding back the latest period tests the model on time it never saw; random folds repeat the mixing.
Exam cue: for predictions about the future, ask for out-of-time testing; a random split across periods overstates performance.

questions.subtopic: 2A Data management for AI. Public benchmarks
questions.question: A Serbian insurance broker picked a language model to review policy wording for its 91% score on public Serbian policy-review exercises, with model answers, posted online since 2019. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: The model may have seen the exercises and answers during training
options.B: The public exercises may not match the broker's own policy wording
options.C: No external assessor confirmed the 91% score for the broker
options.D: The vendor may update the model after the broker signs

questions.key_concept: Public benchmarks can leak into a large model's training data, so scores on them may reflect memorization rather than ability.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the model could have seen the test items before, not only whether they look like real work.
questions.correct_explanation: An exercise set posted online for years is likely to have been swept into a large model's training data, so a high score may show memory of the answers rather than skill at reviewing policy wording. That makes the 91% unreliable as evidence. A gap between the public exercises and the broker's own wording matters too, but it limits how far a valid score applies; contamination may make the score meaningless.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a test should resemble real use. But these exercises already are policy reviews; a fit gap narrows a valid score, whereas contamination may void it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because independent confirmation helps. But an assessor rerunning the same public exercises would reproduce the same possibly memorized score.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because hosted models change. But that is a change-control concern for later; the question is whether today's score proves anything.

tips: Eliminate: C would rerun the same exposed exercises and confirm nothing new, and D is a later change-control issue, not about this evidence.
Final two: A beats B because exercises already in the training data may make the score invalid; a wording mismatch only narrows a valid result.
Exam cue: a high score on a long-public benchmark may reflect memorization; ask for tests on fresh, unpublished cases from real use.

questions.question: An Albanian municipality runs every AI model through the same short release checklist, from its tourist-information chatbot to a model flagging welfare claims for fraud review. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Add group fairness tests to the shared checklist for every model
options.B: Require deeper evidence and independent validation for the welfare model
options.C: Have the IS auditor sign off each welfare-model release
options.D: Keep the checklist and monitor welfare flags monthly after release

questions.key_concept: Lifecycle gates are proportionate: models with higher risk, judged by likelihood and impact including harm to people, need more evidence and independent review.
questions.pre_read: Compare who could be harmed by each model, then ask whether the controls differ.
questions.correct_explanation: A model that sends people's welfare claims to fraud review can cut off support, so it needs stronger evidence before release than a tourist chatbot: data fitness, group results and validation independent of its builders. Gate depth should rise with the likelihood and severity of harm. Monthly monitoring is needed too, but it finds problems after claimants have been flagged; it cannot replace a proportionate gate before release.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because group testing is an AI control. But one added test keeps a uniform gate; the welfare model still lacks the deeper evidence and independent validation it needs.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the IS auditor adds independence. But signing off releases is a management control; the IS auditor assesses the gates and does not operate them.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because monitoring catches drift. But it detects harm after release; a high-impact model needs proportionate evidence before it goes live.

tips: Eliminate: A adds one test to a uniform checklist instead of deepening the welfare model's gate, and C makes the IS auditor operate a release control that management owns.
Final two: B beats D because harm from a fraud flag lands on people at release; monitoring afterward detects it but does not prevent it.
Exam cue: one gate for every model is a design flaw; expect gate depth and independence to rise with risk, counting the likelihood and severity of harm to people.

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. Bought models and gates
questions.question: A Namibian mining company will use a vendor's hosted haul-truck maintenance model; the project lead says the vendor's lifecycle gates make the company's own gates unnecessary. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Accept the vendor's gates and file its release notes as evidence
options.B: Have the IS auditor validate the model before the contract is signed
options.C: Run the company's own gates, using vendor evidence as one input
options.D: Obtain an independent certification of the vendor's development process

questions.key_concept: A vendor's lifecycle does not replace the buyer's: the organization's gates test fitness for its own use, with vendor evidence as one input.
questions.pre_read: Ask whose purpose and data each set of gates was designed to test.
questions.correct_explanation: The vendor's gates test the model against the vendor's purposes and data, not this company's trucks, sites and tolerance for missed failures. The company stays accountable, so its own gates must check fitness for its use, drawing on vendor evidence where useful. A certification of the vendor's process is useful input, but it shows the process is followed, not that the model suits the company's fleet.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the vendor knows its model. But release notes are vendor claims about the vendor's purposes; they do not test fitness for this company's use.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the IS auditor is independent. But validating the model is management's control; the IS auditor assesses whether the gates work.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because certification adds independence. But it confirms the vendor follows its process, not that the model fits this company's trucks and sites.

tips: Eliminate: A treats vendor claims as assurance, and B makes the IS auditor perform validation that belongs to management.
Final two: C beats D because only the company's own gates test fitness for its use; a process certificate covers the vendor's process.
Exam cue: buying a model does not buy out the lifecycle; the organization's gates still apply, with vendor evidence as input.

questions.question: A Kyrgyz television broadcaster fine-tuned a vendor's licensed language model to write subtitles; its model card describes the tuning data but nothing about the base model. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: The tuning data may be too small to change the model's behavior
options.B: The model card was written by the team that tuned the model
options.C: Scores were not compared with the base model's published scores
options.D: Base-model limits and risks pass undocumented into the tuned model

questions.key_concept: Fine-tuning inherits the base model's data, biases and limits, so the tuned model's documentation must cover the base model too.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the tuned model was built on, and whether anyone has documented that layer.
questions.correct_explanation: Fine-tuning adjusts a pre-trained model; it does not remove what the base model learned, including its biases, gaps or unsafe behaviors. A model card that describes only the tuning data leaves those inherited limits unknown to anyone relying on the subtitle model. Comparing scores with the base model's published results is a useful check, but published scores are inputs and say nothing about the base model's data or limits.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because small tuning sets change little. But that would make the base model's undocumented behavior matter more, not less.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because independence sounds important. But builders normally write model cards; independent validation is a separate step.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because comparison shows improvement. But published scores are inputs, not documentation, and reveal nothing about the base model's data or known limits.

tips: Eliminate: A would make the base model matter more, not less, and B confuses documentation, which builders write, with independent validation.
Final two: D beats C because a score comparison cannot reveal inherited data, bias or limits; only documentation covering the base model can.
Exam cue: a tuned model inherits its base model; its documentation must cover both the tuning and what it was built on.

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. Model cards after retraining
questions.question: A Mozambican cashew processor has retrained its kernel-grading model eight times, but the model card describes the launch version; the team says updating it would slow sprints. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Make an updated model card a condition of each release
options.B: Fully rewrite the model card at each annual model review
options.C: Keep the launch card, since the model's code has not changed
options.D: Have the IS auditor maintain the model card between releases

questions.key_concept: Every retrained version needs current documentation; tying the model card to each release keeps it accurate without slowing delivery.
questions.pre_read: Ask which version the documentation describes, and which version is running.
questions.correct_explanation: Each retraining produces a new model whose performance, data and limits may differ, so a card describing the launch version misleads graders, validators and auditors about the model in use. Making an updated card part of each release keeps documentation in step with the model at little cost. An annual rewrite is better than nothing, but for most of the year people would rely on a card that describes an older model.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it is less work for the team. But between reviews, users rely on a card describing an older model that may behave differently.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the code is stable. But a retrained model is a new model; its data, results and limits change even when the code does not.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the IS auditor values documentation. But maintaining it is the team's job; the IS auditor assesses documentation and does not write it.

tips: Eliminate: C treats the model as code alone, and D gives the IS auditor a documentation task the model team owns.
Final two: A beats B because every retraining is a new model; documentation tied to each release stays accurate, while an annual rewrite lags.
Exam cue: agile does not mean undocumented; expect documentation updates built into each model release.

questions.subtopic: 2B AI lifecycle. Models that feed models
questions.question: An Uzbek cotton cooperative is retiring its soil-moisture model, whose daily scores are one input to its separate irrigation-scheduling model. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Archive the soil-moisture model's versions, logs and settings
options.B: Have the irrigation model's owner assess and retest it before switch-off
options.C: Let the irrigation pipeline fill missing scores with recent averages
options.D: Retire the irrigation model at the same time to avoid a gap

questions.key_concept: Retirement starts by finding what depends on a model's outputs; a downstream model that loses an input must be assessed and retested.
questions.pre_read: Ask what consumes the retiring model's outputs, and whether any of it is another model.
questions.correct_explanation: Removing an input changes what the irrigation model sees, so its behavior after the switch-off is untested. Its owner should assess the dependency and retest or adapt the model first, or fields may be watered on wrong schedules. Archiving the retired model's versions and logs is part of a sound retirement, but it protects records; it does nothing for the live model that still depends on the scores.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because retirement must keep records. But archiving protects past evidence; it does not stop the dependent irrigation model misbehaving after switch-off.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it keeps the pipeline running. But averaged scores are invented inputs; the model would run on data it was never tested with.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it avoids a broken input. But it removes a working model without a replacement and leaves irrigation decisions unsupported.

tips: Eliminate: C feeds the model invented inputs, and D retires a working model to avoid a dependency instead of managing it.
Final two: B beats A because the live irrigation model depends on the retiring scores; records can be archived, but the dependency must be tested first.
Exam cue: before switching off a model, find what depends on its outputs, including other models.

Retraining on today's courses may come later, but it makes a new model that must pass the gates, and only after the owner decides the model has a future.

wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the program has ended. But deleting the model and its data loses records needed to answer challenges, and skips the owner's decision and dependent systems.

questions.question: A Panamanian hospital network widened the training window of its missed-appointment model from 12 to 36 months, logging it as a configuration tweak outside change management. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.C: Test and approve the retrained model as a change before use

questions.pre_read: Ask what changed in what the model learned from, not only in the code.
questions.correct_explanation: Older history can carry patterns that no longer hold, such as attendance habits from before a clinic moved or changed its hours, so a wider window produces a new model whose behavior can shift with the code untouched. It is a change: the retrained model needs testing against acceptance criteria and the owner's approval before use. Recording it in the change calendar gives visibility, but an untested, unapproved model can still go live.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because nothing in the code moved. But the training window decides what the model learns; changing it changes the model.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it restores the old state. But the wider window may be better; the gap is that nobody tested or approved it, not the choice itself.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it records the change. But visibility is not control; an untested, unapproved model can still reach production.

tips: Eliminate: A treats the model as code alone, and B reverses a setting that may be sound instead of controlling it.
Final two: C beats D because logging a change does not test or approve it; only testing and approval stop a worse model going live.
Exam cue: the data a model learns from is part of the model; changing the training window, sample or labels is a change.

questions.question: A Honduran rental agency's change advisory board approved a retrained tenant-screening model because its overall accuracy rose two points; no other results were presented. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Higher accuracy may hide worse errors for some groups of applicants
options.B: A two-point gain is too small to justify a new release
options.C: Accuracy may decline later as applicants' circumstances change
options.D: The approvers did not compare the model with a vendor benchmark

questions.key_concept: Approving an AI change on overall accuracy alone can hide worse errors for some groups; approval evidence needs error types and group results.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the single number averages over, and who could be worse off inside it.
questions.correct_explanation: Overall accuracy averages across everyone and every type of error, so a two-point gain can coexist with more wrongful rejections for women, self-employed or older applicants. Approving on that number alone means nobody checked the errors that matter or results by group. Later decline as circumstances change is a real risk, but it is a monitoring question; the approval itself rests on evidence that cannot show the model is fit.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because small gains may not be worth the risk. But size is not the issue; even a large gain in overall accuracy could hide group harm.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because models drift. But that is for production monitoring; the concern now is that the approval evidence cannot show the model is fit.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because benchmarks add context. But a vendor benchmark is another overall score; it does not show errors by group or type.

tips: Eliminate: B debates the size of a gain in a metric that cannot show fitness, and D swaps one overall score for another.
Final two: A beats C because the approval itself rests on an average that can hide group harm; later drift is a monitoring concern.
Exam cue: a change approved on overall accuracy alone is weakly evidenced; expect error types and group results before approval.

questions.question: A monthly baseline check finds a Qatari bank's mortgage-help chatbot running with a higher temperature setting and a different retrieval index than approved; its answers look normal. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Update the approved baseline to match the settings now in use
options.B: Restore the approved settings at once and close the baseline check
options.C: Run the baseline check weekly so differences surface sooner
options.D: Treat the differences as unauthorized changes and trace their cause

questions.key_concept: AI configuration baselines include model settings and retrieval sources; unexplained differences are investigated as unauthorized changes.
questions.pre_read: Ask how the live settings came to differ from the approved ones, and who changed them.
questions.correct_explanation: Settings such as temperature and the retrieval index change what a chatbot says as surely as a code release, and these differ from the approved baseline. Until a change record explains them, they are unauthorized changes: change control was bypassed or failed, and the cause must be found. Restoring the approved settings may be right, but doing it and closing the check loses the chance to learn who changed what, and why.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because nothing looks broken. But approving unknown changes after the fact rewards bypassing change control and leaves untested settings live.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it returns to a known state. But closing without finding how the settings changed leaves the gap open to recur.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because faster detection helps. But it changes when differences are found, not what is done about this one.

tips: Eliminate: A approves unknown changes after the fact, and C speeds up detection without dealing with the difference already found.
Final two: D beats B because an unexplained difference is an unauthorized change; restoring settings without finding the cause lets it recur.
Exam cue: AI settings such as temperature, prompts and indexes are part of the baseline; unexplained differences are unauthorized changes.

questions.question: A Pakistani surgical-instrument maker's polish-defect model has a documented rollback to version 7, but its feature pipeline no longer produces two inputs that version 7 needs. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Keep version 7's documentation ready for use in a rollback
options.B: Rehearse the version 7 rollback now and fix what fails
options.C: Have the data team rebuild the inputs when a rollback is needed
options.D: Drop rollback and retrain a fix quickly whenever a release fails

questions.key_concept: A rollback counts only once rehearsed on the current pipeline; the older version must still run with the features and settings it needs.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the older version could actually run today, not just whether a rollback is written down.
questions.correct_explanation: A rollback restores a previous model with the inputs and settings it depends on, and version 7 cannot run on today's pipeline. Rehearsing the rollback now forces the two missing inputs to be restored and shows whether anything else fails, so the rollback is proven before an incident. Rebuilding the inputs only when a rollback is needed puts untested engineering on the critical path while defective instruments may be passing inspection.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because documented rollbacks look ready. But documentation does not make version 7 runnable without the inputs it needs.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the inputs can be rebuilt. But doing it under incident pressure is slow and untested, while defective instruments may pass inspection.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because retraining fixes behavior. But a rushed retrain is an untested change; rollback exists to restore a known approved state.

tips: Eliminate: A documents a rollback that cannot run, and D replaces a known approved state with a rushed, untested retrain.
Final two: B beats C because a rehearsal now restores the missing inputs and proves the rollback works; rebuilding them during an incident is slow, untested work.
Exam cue: a documented rollback is not evidence until it has been rehearsed on today's pipeline.

questions.subtopic: 2C AI change management. Embedding model swap
questions.question: An Argentine soccer club's member assistant searches documents indexed with a vendor's embedding model; after a vendor swap, queries and new documents use a new model. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Pin the version of the model that writes the assistant's answers
options.B: Rely on the vendor's testing of its new embedding model
options.C: Reindex all documents and regression-test search as a change
options.D: Track members' complaints about wrong answers for a month

questions.key_concept: Swapping an embedding model changes retrieval; mixed indexes need reindexing and regression testing like any other model change.
questions.pre_read: Identify which component the vendor changed before choosing which control fits.
questions.correct_explanation: Embeddings from different models are not comparable, so queries encoded by the new model match poorly against documents encoded by the old one; much of the library may silently drop out of search. That makes the swap a change to the system: reindex the documents and rerun regression tests on retrieval before relying on it. Pinning the answer-writing model is sound practice, but that component did not change.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because pinning controls vendor updates. But the change was to the embedding model, not the answer model; pinning the wrong component leaves search broken.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the vendor tests its releases. But the vendor cannot test the club's mixed index; customers must test updates against their own use.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because complaints reveal problems. But members may never notice missing documents; waiting for complaints detects harm late.

tips: Eliminate: B relies on the vendor's testing of its own release, and D waits for complaints about missing answers members may not notice.
Final two: C beats A because the changed component is the embedding model; pinning the answer model protects a part that did not move.
Exam cue: a vendor change to any component, such as embeddings, is a change to your AI system; test it on your own use.

questions.question: A Zimbabwean safari-lodge group uses a hosted model for booking chats under the vendor's standard terms, which allow unannounced model updates and offer no version pinning. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Run regression tests on a schedule and monitor output patterns
options.B: Accept the terms, since a vendor tests its own model updates
options.C: Have the IS auditor review the vendor's release notes each month
options.D: Revalidate the hosted model completely at each annual review

questions.key_concept: When a contract cannot stop silent vendor updates, the owner detects them with scheduled regression tests and output monitoring.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the contract lets the group prevent updates; if not, ask how it would notice one.
questions.correct_explanation: Under these terms the vendor can change the model any day without warning, so the group cannot prevent silent updates; it can only detect them quickly. A fixed regression test set run on a schedule, plus monitoring of output patterns such as escalation or refusal rates, shows when behavior shifts so the owner can respond. A full annual revalidation is thorough but would leave months of undetected change between reviews.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because vendors do test. But the vendor tests against its own goals, not this group's booking chats; customers must test updates against their own use.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the IS auditor is independent. But detecting changes is the owner's operating control, and unannounced updates may have no release notes.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because full validation is rigorous. But updates can arrive any week; an annual check leaves months of silent change undetected.

tips: Eliminate: B relies on the vendor's testing of its own release, and C makes the IS auditor run an operating control the owner needs.
Final two: A beats D because silent updates can land any week; frequent regression tests and monitoring catch them, while annual revalidation comes too late.
Exam cue: when updates cannot be prevented by contract, expect frequent detection: scheduled regression tests and output monitoring.

questions.question: Guatemalan insurance claims officers review a model's health-claim hold recommendations; their bonus counts cases cleared daily, and the model's choice comes pre-selected, so agreeing takes one click. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Add a monthly supervisor check of cases where officers agreed
options.B: Train officers on how the model scores health claims
options.C: Raise the model's threshold so that fewer health claims need review
options.D: Make overriding the model no costlier for officers than agreeing

questions.key_concept: Oversight fails when incentives make agreeing with the model cheaper than overriding it; overriding must cost reviewers no more than agreeing.
questions.pre_read: Trace the steps and the reward for an officer who agrees with the model, then for one who overrides it.
questions.correct_explanation: The design pays officers to agree: confirming the pre-selected hold takes one click and adds to their daily count, while overriding takes longer and slows it. That pushes them toward the model's recommendations, which is automation bias built into the design. Making overriding no costlier than agreeing, with no pre-selected answer and no bonus penalty, lets oversight work. Training helps officers understand the model, but trained officers still face incentives that reward agreeing.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because samples check quality. But it reviews after claimants are affected and leaves the incentive that drives agreement unchanged.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because understanding the model is needed for oversight. But knowledge does not help if overriding still costs officers time and bonus.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because fewer reviews ease workload. But it reduces human review instead of fixing why reviewers defer to the model.

tips: Eliminate: A checks agreed cases after claimants are affected, and C cuts the number of reviews rather than fixing their quality.
Final two: D beats B because training cannot outweigh a design that rewards agreeing; oversight needs overriding to cost no more than agreeing.
Exam cue: when reviewers are rewarded for speed and agreeing is the default, expect rubber-stamping; fix the design, not just the reviewer.

questions.question: An Algerian refinery's model assigns crews to equipment alarms; dispatchers can change single assignments, but no one may suspend the model when its assignments look wrong. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Let dispatchers change more assignments without a supervisor's agreement
options.B: Let a named owner suspend the model through a tested procedure
options.C: Give the IS auditor authority to suspend the model when needed
options.D: Retrain the model whenever dispatchers change many assignments

questions.key_concept: Human oversight includes authority to stop the whole system, not only override single outputs; it needs a named owner and a tested fallback.
questions.pre_read: Separate fixing one output from stopping the system, and ask who can do each.
questions.correct_explanation: Changing single assignments is oversight of individual outputs, but when the model goes wrong broadly, case-by-case fixes cannot keep up. Someone must hold authority, and a tested way, to suspend the model and fall back to manual dispatch: a human in command. Giving dispatchers freer overrides strengthens case-level review, yet still leaves no one able to stop the system as a whole.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because easier overrides improve oversight. But it still works one assignment at a time; nobody can stop a model that is wrong across the board.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the IS auditor is independent. But suspending a model is an operating decision for its owner; the IS auditor assesses whether that authority exists.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because retraining addresses errors. But it is a slow change, not a stop control, and many overrides need investigation first.

tips: Eliminate: C gives the IS auditor an operating decision, and D answers the need for a stop control with a slow model change.
Final two: B beats A because overriding single outputs cannot halt a model that is wrong across the board; someone must be able to stop it.
Exam cue: oversight has levels; besides overriding single decisions, check that a named person can suspend the whole system.

questions.question: A Cambodian province retrains its malaria-spraying model monthly; its dashboard shows drift and district error rates, but no reading triggers action, as the team relies on retraining. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the owner set a threshold and response for each indicator
options.B: Send the dashboard to the board each month for its review
options.C: Have the IS auditor set alert thresholds for each indicator
options.D: Rely on monthly retraining to correct drift as it builds up

questions.key_concept: AI monitoring indicators need owner-set thresholds within approved tolerance and a defined response when breached.
questions.pre_read: Ask what reading would make someone act, and what they would then do.
questions.correct_explanation: Indicators without thresholds tell no one when to act, so drift or district error rates can worsen while everyone watches. The model owner should set thresholds inside the tolerance senior management approved, each tied to a response such as review, retraining through change control or disengagement. Sending the dashboard to the board raises visibility, but without thresholds the board has no basis for deciding when a reading needs action.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because board reporting shows seriousness. But raw readings with no thresholds give the board no trigger for action either.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the IS auditor is objective. But setting thresholds is the owner's decision within approved tolerance; the IS auditor assesses them.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because retraining refreshes the model. But scheduled retraining measures nothing and can learn from drifted or bad data; it does not replace thresholds that trigger review.

tips: Eliminate: C has the IS auditor set operating thresholds that the owner sets, and D trusts scheduled retraining that measures nothing.
Final two: A beats B because the owner, within approved tolerance, decides when a reading needs action and what follows; raw readings sent to the board trigger nothing.
Exam cue: a key risk indicator needs a threshold and a response; a dashboard of numbers with neither is monitoring in name only.

questions.question: An Iraqi freight platform's carrier-vetting model rejects 30% of trucking firms' applications; its monitoring tracks cargo theft only among carriers it approved. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: Theft by approved carriers may take many months to come to light
options.B: Shippers may report theft by approved carriers inconsistently
options.C: Wrongful rejections never appear in the data being monitored
options.D: A 30% rejection rate is too high for a vetting model

questions.key_concept: Monitoring that observes outcomes only for approved cases cannot see wrongful rejections; the screened-out population needs its own checks.
questions.pre_read: Ask whose outcomes the monitoring can ever observe, and whose it never can.
questions.correct_explanation: The model's outcomes are observed only for carriers it let through, so the rejected 30% are invisible: an honest firm wrongly turned away never produces a record showing the model was wrong. Monitoring can look healthy while wrongful rejections, possibly concentrated in some regions or groups, go unseen. Slow theft reports delay the signal, but it still arrives for approved carriers; for rejected applicants it never arrives.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because lagging outcomes slow monitoring. But the signal does arrive for approved carriers; for rejected applicants it never arrives.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because reports can be uneven. But the stem gives no sign of it, and better reports would still say nothing about rejected applicants.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the rate looks high. But a high rejection rate may suit the risk; the concern is that rejection errors are never measured.

tips: Eliminate: B rests on reporting problems the stem never mentions, and D judges the rejection rate without any basis.
Final two: C beats A because slow theft reports still arrive for approved carriers; for rejected applicants no outcome is ever observed.
Exam cue: if outcomes are seen only for cases the model approved, monitoring cannot see its wrongful rejections; look for ways to test them.
