questions.question: An Indonesian motorcycle-finance company's chatbot, presented as a staff member named Sari, decides whether borrowers get extensions on loan repayments. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have a supervisor review a weekly sample of borrowers' extension cases
options.B: Have Sari explain each extension decision in more detail
options.C: Post a general notice telling borrowers the company uses AI
options.D: Tell borrowers an AI system decides and how to reach a person

questions.key_concept: People affected by an AI decision must be told AI was involved and how to reach a person who can review and change it.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a borrower believes about who decided, and what they could do if they disagreed.
questions.correct_explanation: Borrowers who think a staff member named Sari decided their extension have no reason to ask for human review, and no route to one. Telling them that an AI system makes the decision, and how to reach a staff member who can change it, gives affected people the means to challenge it. A weekly supervisor sample adds oversight, but borrowers still cannot see that a machine decided or seek review of their own case.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because sampling adds oversight. But it reviews a few cases after the fact; borrowers still do not know an AI decided or how to challenge it.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because reasons help borrowers. But reasons from an apparent staff member hide that an AI decided, and still give no route to a person.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it discloses AI use. But a general notice does not tell each borrower their own decision was automated or how to seek review.

tips: Eliminate: B adds reasons while borrowers still think a person decided, and C gives a general notice that does not reach each decision.
Final two: D beats A because sampling oversees some decisions, but only disclosure and a route to a person let each borrower challenge their own.
Exam cue: affected people can challenge an AI decision only if they know an AI was involved and how to reach someone who can change it.

questions.question: A Paraguayan power cooperative's discount-tariff eligibility model logs the factors behind each decision, yet every rejected applicant gets the same three 'main reasons', whatever their application showed. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Check the three reasons against the model's top global features
options.B: Give applicants the specific reasons for their own cases
options.C: Stop sending reasons, since generic ones may mislead applicants
options.D: Refer applicants to the model's vendor for case explanations

questions.key_concept: Explanations to affected people must be local: specific to their own decision and traceable to the log, not the model's global feature importance.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the explanation would differ between two applicants with different applications.
questions.correct_explanation: Identical reasons for everyone explain nothing about any one rejection, so applicants cannot tell what to challenge or correct. Each applicant should get the reasons recorded for their own decision, drawn from the decision log, so an appeal can address their actual application. Confirming the three reasons match the model's top global features shows what drives the model overall, but a global explanation still cannot say which factors decided one case.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it checks the reasons are real model drivers. But global feature importance describes the model overall, not which factors decided one applicant's case.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because misleading reasons cause harm. But no reasons leave applicants less able to challenge; the fix is accurate reasons, not none.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the vendor built the model. But the cooperative owns its decisions and must explain them; a vendor has no duty to applicants.

tips: Eliminate: C removes reasons instead of correcting them, and D passes the cooperative's duty to explain its own decisions to a vendor.
Final two: B beats A because only local, case-specific reasons let an applicant challenge their own decision; global feature importance explains the model, not the case.
Exam cue: an explanation helps an affected person only if it is specific to their decision and traceable to the log.

questions.question: An Azerbaijani pipeline operator's corrosion model will choose which pipe sections get inspected; under 2% are corroded, and the draft acceptance criterion is 95% overall accuracy. What should the IS auditor recommend as MOST important?

options.A: Add a cap on missed corroded sections, set from risk tolerance
options.B: Raise the overall accuracy pass mark from 95% to 99%
options.C: Require the model to flag at least 2% of pipe sections
options.D: Use the vendor's published accuracy figure as the criterion

questions.key_concept: When the outcome is rare, acceptance criteria must target the costly error, such as missed cases, not overall accuracy.
questions.pre_read: Ask which error would hurt most here, and whether the criterion measures that error at all.
questions.correct_explanation: With under 2% of sections corroded, a model that flags nothing scores over 98% accuracy, so the 95% criterion can pass a model that misses every corroded pipe. The error that matters is a missed corroded section, so the criterion should cap that rate, set from risk tolerance. Raising the bar to 99% still lets a model pass while missing half or more of the corroded sections.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a higher bar seems stricter. But with under 2% corroded, 99% accuracy can still miss half or more of them; the measure is the problem.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it matches the corrosion rate. But a model can flag 2% of sections and still pick mostly sound pipes; volume is not detection.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because vendor figures are ready-made. But they are inputs, measured on other data, and still an overall figure.

tips: Eliminate: C sets a flagging quota that says nothing about which pipes are found, and D borrows an overall figure measured on someone else's data.
Final two: A beats B because with rare corrosion, overall accuracy stays high while corroded sections are missed; only a cap on misses measures that error.
Exam cue: when the event is rare, overall accuracy flatters; set criteria on the costly error, such as missed cases.

questions.question: A Cameroonian parliament's clerks approved a debate summarizer after each read about 20 outputs, keeping no record of inputs or results; the vendor updates the model monthly. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: About 20 outputs per clerk is too small a test sample
options.B: The clerks may lack the technical skill to test an AI model
options.C: No fixed test cases exist to rerun after each model change
options.D: The tool was not tested on the vendor's standard benchmark

questions.key_concept: Approval of a generative AI tool needs recorded test cases and results; unrecorded spot reads give no baseline for the approval or for later updates.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the parliament could rerun next month to see whether the tool got worse.
questions.correct_explanation: Generative output varies and the vendor changes the model monthly, so the parliament needs a fixed, recorded set of test cases with expected qualities that can be rerun after each update. Without one, nothing shows how the tool performed or whether an update made it worse. Twenty outputs per clerk may also be too few, but even a larger informal read would leave nothing to rerun.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because small samples are weak. But a larger unrecorded read would still leave nothing to compare after each monthly update.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because AI testing can be technical. But clerks who know the debates are the right judges of summary accuracy; domain expertise is what this test needs.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because benchmarks are standardized. But a vendor benchmark measures general ability, not accurate summaries of these debates.

tips: Eliminate: B doubts the domain experts best placed to judge summaries, and D swaps the parliament's own use for a general benchmark.
Final two: C beats A because a bigger informal sample still cannot be rerun; a recorded test set lets each monthly update be checked.
Exam cue: for generative AI that changes often, look for a documented, rerunnable test set; unrecorded spot reads give no baseline.

questions.question: A Greek supermarket chain's self-checkout theft model flags men and women, and younger and older shoppers, at similar rates, yet women aged over 70 file most complaints. Which result should the IS auditor request FIRST?

options.A: Flag rates for women and for over-70s, each on this year's data
options.B: Overall accuracy on recent confirmed theft cases
options.C: The vendor's fairness benchmark for self-checkout theft detection
options.D: Wrongful-flag rates for combined groups such as older women

questions.key_concept: Fairness by single attributes can hide gaps in combined groups, such as older women; test the intersections that the evidence points to.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether groups tested one attribute at a time could hide a smaller group where they overlap.
questions.correct_explanation: Similar flag rates by sex and by age can hide a gap where the two meet: a model can treat women, and older shoppers, fairly on average while wrongly flagging older women far more often. The complaints point to that combined group, so wrongful-flag rates for intersections such as older women are the result that can confirm or rule out the gap. Recalculating each attribute alone repeats the averaging that hides it.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it targets the complaining groups. But rates for women alone and for over-70s alone average over older women, so the gap stays hidden.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because accuracy on confirmed cases matters. But an overall figure says nothing about how any one group is treated, least of all a small combined group.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because benchmarks are ready-made. But a vendor benchmark uses other data and shoppers; it cannot show how this chain's older female shoppers are treated.

tips: Eliminate: B gives one overall figure, and C borrows a benchmark built on other data and other shoppers.
Final two: D beats A because gaps can sit where groups combine; rates for each attribute alone average them away.
Exam cue: fair results for each attribute alone do not prove fairness for combined groups; test the intersections the evidence points to.

questions.question: A Maltese health service's fall-risk model misses falls among wheelchair users no more often than among others, but the test held 25 wheelchair users among 40,000 patients. What is the IS auditor's BEST conclusion?

options.A: The model treats wheelchair users as fairly as other patients
options.B: The test is too small to show reliably how wheelchair users fare
options.C: The model is likely biased and needs retraining on more wheelchair users
options.D: The overall miss rate across 40,000 patients settles the question

questions.key_concept: Group fairness results need enough cases per group; with very few, the right conclusion is that fairness is not yet shown.
questions.pre_read: Count how many people the group result rests on before reading the rate.
questions.correct_explanation: With only 25 wheelchair users, one or two extra missed falls would change their rate sharply, so matching the average proves little either way. The sound conclusion is that the test cannot yet show how these patients fare; a larger, targeted sample is needed before anyone concludes the model is fair or unfair. Calling it biased and retraining assumes a problem the evidence has not shown.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the rates match. But 25 people are too few for the match to mean much; the result could easily differ in use.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because small groups are often underserved. But the evidence does not show bias; it shows the test cannot tell either way.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because 40,000 is large. But an overall rate is dominated by other patients and can hide how a small group fares.

tips: Eliminate: A reads a match on 25 people as proof, and D lets 40,000 other patients stand in for a small group.
Final two: B beats C because the evidence is too thin to show bias either way; concluding the model is biased goes beyond it.
Exam cue: check group sizes before trusting group results; a tiny group's rate supports no conclusion, good or bad.

questions.question: A Cypriot sports-betting regulator's validators received only the builders' summary metrics for a new match-fixing alert model; their requests for its data and code were refused. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Give validators the data and code access that challenge requires
options.B: Have validators recompute the builders' summary metrics for errors
options.C: Have the IS auditor review the code in the validators' place
options.D: Accept the builders' summary, as their tests cover the same ground

questions.key_concept: Independent validation needs access to the model's data, code and design; validators limited to builders' summaries cannot challenge the model.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the validators could actually examine, not only who they report to.
questions.correct_explanation: Independent validation means challenging the model, its data, design and code, not checking the builders' arithmetic. Without access, validators can only restate what the builders chose to report, so the validation is independent in name only. Recomputing the summary metrics confirms the sums but not whether the data, labels or method behind them are sound, which is where weaknesses in an alert model usually hide.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because recomputation is a real check. But it confirms the builders' arithmetic, not the data, labels or design behind the numbers.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the IS auditor is independent. But validation is a management control; the IS auditor assesses it and does not perform it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because builders test their work. But builders' testing is never independent validation; their summary is what needs challenge.

tips: Eliminate: C makes the IS auditor perform validation, and D treats the builders' own testing as independent validation.
Final two: A beats B because effective challenge needs the data and code; recomputing a summary only checks the builders' arithmetic.
Exam cue: independent validators need access as well as independence; without data and code, validation only restates the builders' report.

questions.question: An Armenian robo-advice firm's investment assistant was red-teamed only by security engineers, who tested data theft and system-prompt leaks. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST before launch?

options.A: Repeat the same security red team after each model update
options.B: Rely on the vendor's filter to block harmful replies to customers
options.C: Have the IS auditor red-team the assistant before it launches
options.D: Add unsuitable-advice scenarios, judged by investment specialists

questions.key_concept: Red teaming covers harmful outputs to the system's own users, judged by domain specialists, not only data theft by attackers.
questions.pre_read: Ask how the assistant could hurt the customers who use it exactly as intended.
questions.correct_explanation: Security engineers test whether attackers can steal data, but for an investment assistant a likely harm is advice that is wrong or unsuitable for the customer, such as pushing risky products on a retiree. Red teaming should include those harmful-output scenarios, judged by specialists who know what suitable advice looks like. Repeating the security-only red team after updates keeps it current but still never tests the harm customers are most exposed to.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because retesting after change is good practice. But it repeats tests that never covered harmful advice, so the main customer harm stays untested.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because filters block harmful text. But a filter tuned for offensive content will not spot advice that is polite, fluent and unsuitable.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the IS auditor is independent. But red teaming is a test the owner commissions; the IS auditor assesses its scope and results.

tips: Eliminate: B trusts a content filter to judge suitability, and C makes the IS auditor perform testing that the owner commissions.
Final two: D beats A because the untested harm is unsuitable advice to customers; repeating security-only tests keeps that gap open.
Exam cue: red teaming covers how a system can harm its own users, judged by people who know the domain, not only attacks by outsiders.

questions.question: A Lao forestry department's illegal-logging model retrains weekly on villagers' app photos, using the labels villagers choose themselves. Which threat should the IS auditor consider MOST significant?

options.A: Rival groups copying the model by querying it repeatedly
options.B: Altered photos fooling the model at the moment they are scored
options.C: Mislabeled photos teaching the model to miss illegal logging
options.D: Mass uploads of labeled photos slowing the app for others

questions.key_concept: When untrusted users supply training data or labels for regular retraining, poisoning is the leading threat.
questions.pre_read: Ask who can influence what the model learns, not only what it scores.
questions.correct_explanation: Because villagers choose the labels and the model retrains on them every week, anyone with the app can shape what it learns: people profiting from logging could label clear-cut sites as normal forest until the model stops flagging them. That is data poisoning, and it changes the model for every future decision. Altered photos that fool the model at scoring time succeed one decision at a time; they do not change the model itself.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because extraction is a known threat. But nothing suggests open scoring access, and a copied logging model offers little gain.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because evasion is common. But it fools one decision at a time; open labels feeding weekly retraining change the model itself.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because uploads are open. But slow service is an availability issue; it does not corrupt what the model learns.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes open scoring access the stem never describes, and D slows the service without changing what the model learns.
Final two: C beats B because labels feeding retraining change the model for everyone; evasion fools single decisions.
Exam cue: when untrusted users supply training labels, poisoning is the first threat to weigh.

questions.question: A Senegalese recipe site's chatbot allows users 30 prompts an hour; overnight, a few accounts filled their quotas with pasted whole cookbooks, exhausting the monthly model budget. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Raise the model usage budget agreed with the vendor
options.B: Cap prompt length and daily token use per account, with alerts
options.C: Lower each user's limit from 30 prompts an hour to 10
options.D: Block the accounts involved and keep the current prompt limits

questions.key_concept: Public AI services need per-user token and input-size limits, because model cost follows tokens and attackers can exhaust it: a denial of AI service.
questions.pre_read: Ask what one user could cost the service, and what stops them.
questions.correct_explanation: Model cost grows with the tokens in each prompt, so a count of prompts does not bound spending: a few accounts sent huge prompts within their quota and exhausted the budget, a denial of AI service. Capping prompt length and token use per account, with alerts on unusual use, bounds what any user can consume. A lower hourly prompt limit cuts the number of prompts, not their size.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because more budget restores service. But it raises the cost of the next attack without preventing it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because tighter limits slow abuse. But cost follows tokens, not prompt count; ten whole cookbooks an hour still drain the budget.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it stops the source. But new accounts are easy to open, and the limits that allowed the attack stay unchanged.

tips: Eliminate: A pays for the attack instead of preventing it, and D blocks these accounts while leaving the gap open for new ones.
Final two: B beats C because model cost follows prompt size; a lower prompt count still lets each prompt carry a whole book.
Exam cue: for public generative AI, limit tokens and input size, not only request counts; compute is what attackers exhaust.

questions.question: A Ukrainian grain trader's pricing assistant reads market news websites; it passed prompt-injection tests in which testers typed attacks into its chat window. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Retest it with attack instructions hidden in news web pages
options.B: Rely on the chat tests, since the same model reads both sources
options.C: Block websites from unfamiliar domains at the network firewall
options.D: Filter injected instructions out of the assistant's final answers

questions.key_concept: Direct injection tests do not cover indirect injection through content an assistant reads; each input path needs its own tests.
questions.pre_read: List every source of text the assistant reads, then ask which of them the tests used.
questions.correct_explanation: Reading websites opens a path for indirect prompt injection: anyone who can publish a page, comment or ad can plant instructions the assistant may follow. Typed chat attacks test only the direct path, so they say little about this one. Retesting with instructions hidden in web pages shows what the assistant does with them. Blocking unfamiliar domains narrows exposure, but trusted news sites can carry injected text too.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because one model handles both. But indirect injection arrives inside content the assistant treats as data; the chat tests never tried that path.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it limits sources. But familiar sites can host injected comments or ads, and a firewall cannot read instructions in content.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because filters catch some attacks. But injected instructions can act through the assistant's tools or shape answers without appearing in them.

tips: Eliminate: B treats typed chat tests as covering web content, and D filters answers, which misses instructions acting through tools.
Final two: A beats C because only testing shows how the assistant handles injected web content; blocking domains narrows exposure, but trusted sites can carry injections.
Exam cue: direct and indirect injection are different paths; test every source of text the assistant reads, not only its chat window.

questions.question: An Austrian ski resort's public guest chatbot answers from an internal wiki that all 900 seasonal staff can edit. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Limit the chatbot's admin console to two named engineers
options.B: Place the chatbot behind a web application firewall
options.C: Let only named, reviewed authors change its source pages
options.D: Add an output filter that blocks offensive words in its replies

questions.key_concept: In retrieval-based assistants, anyone who can edit source content can inject instructions, so write access to sources is an AI control.
questions.pre_read: List who can put text in front of the model, including through its sources.
questions.correct_explanation: Every page the chatbot retrieves is text it may treat as instructions, so any of 900 seasonal staff could plant content that steers what guests are told: an indirect prompt injection from inside. Restricting edits of the chatbot's source pages to named authors, with review, controls that path. Locking down the chatbot's admin console protects its settings but leaves the wiki content, where this risk sits, open to every editor.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because admin access is privileged. But the open path is the wiki text the chatbot retrieves, which 900 staff can still edit.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because firewalls protect web apps. But injected text arrives as ordinary content through allowed channels; a firewall cannot judge instructions in it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because offensive replies are visible harm. But injected instructions can mislead guests with polite, false answers that a word filter passes.

tips: Eliminate: B relies on a firewall that cannot read instructions in content, and D blocks rude words while polite, misleading answers pass.
Final two: C beats A because the chatbot takes its answers from wiki text; locking the admin console leaves that path open to 900 editors.
Exam cue: for retrieval-based assistants, whoever can write the source content can steer the answers; control who writes it.

questions.question: A South Korean comics platform's moderation service loads whichever model its registry tags 'production'; code releases need approval, and 60 data scientists have registry write access. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Log every production tag move for review each month
options.B: Encrypt the registry's stored model files at rest
options.C: Confirm that every code release to the moderation service is approved
options.D: Let only the approved release process move the production tag

questions.key_concept: A model registry tag can deploy a model without any code release, so only the approved release process may move it.
questions.pre_read: Ask what actually decides which model runs in production, and who can change it.
questions.correct_explanation: Moving the tag swaps the model that makes moderation decisions without any code release, so in practice the tag is the deployment and registry write access is the power to deploy. With 60 people able to move it, a mistaken or deliberate switch reaches production untested and unapproved. Letting only the approved release process move the tag brings model deployment under change control. Monthly log review finds a harmful switch weeks after it went live.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because logs create accountability. But review a month later finds a harmful switch after it has shaped moderation decisions.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because encryption protects stored files. But it does not limit who can move the production tag, which is what deploys a model.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because code change control is the usual release gate. But moving the tag swaps the model with no code release, so approved code releases never cover it.

tips: Eliminate: B protects stored files but not who can move the tag, and C checks code releases that a tag move bypasses.
Final two: D beats A because restricting who moves the tag prevents untested switches; monthly log review finds them after they act.
Exam cue: in MLOps, a registry tag or alias can be a deployment; whoever can move it can change production AI.

questions.question: An Emirati co-working operator's facilities agent reads supplier emails and, 'to be useful', can order repairs, unlock members' doors and edit contracts at any time. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Tell the agent in its prompt to ask staff before unlocking doors
options.B: Grant task-scoped rights and require approval for high-impact actions
options.C: Review a monthly log of the agent's door, contract and repair activity
options.D: Limit who can send requests to the agent to facility managers

questions.key_concept: AI agents get task-scoped rights and system-enforced approval for high-impact actions; usefulness does not justify broad standing permissions.
questions.pre_read: List what the agent's account could do right now if something steered it wrongly.
questions.correct_explanation: Rights the agent always holds mean anything that steers it, such as an instruction hidden in a supplier email or a plain mistake, can unlock members' doors, order repairs or rewrite contracts at once. Scoping rights to each task and requiring a person's approval, enforced by the systems, for high-impact actions bounds the damage. A monthly log review shows what happened, but only after a door has opened.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it states the rule clearly. But prompt instructions can be overridden by injected text or errors; permissions hold where instructions do not.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because logs show what the agent did. But review weeks later cannot undo an opened door or a changed contract.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it narrows access. But the agent also acts on supplier emails, so injected text can still steer it; the agent's own rights are what need bounding.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on a prompt instruction that injected text can override, and D limits who can message the agent while injected emails still reach it.
Final two: B beats C because scoped rights and approvals prevent high-impact actions; monthly log review only finds them afterward.
Exam cue: 'more useful' is no reason for standing rights; judge an agent by what its account can do, not what it is told.

questions.question: A Montenegrin tax office's AI vendor warned an update may put plausible wrong amounts in tax notices, raising no errors; procurement left it unread for nine days. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Send vendor AI notices to incident intake with named triage roles
options.B: Have procurement check the inbox daily and forward any urgent mail
options.C: Treat vendor notices as change requests for the next release
options.D: Require the vendor to fix flaws before releasing any update

questions.key_concept: Vendor notices about model flaws are AI incident signals and must flow into incident intake with named triage roles.
questions.pre_read: Trace the path a vendor's warning takes before anyone acts on it.
questions.correct_explanation: A vendor warning that its model may misstate tax amounts is an AI incident signal: households may already be receiving wrong notices. Because such errors look normal and trip no alarms, outside signals like vendor notices may be the only early warning. They belong in the incident process, with named roles to triage them by impact on the people affected. Daily inbox checks by procurement still depend on someone spotting the right email.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because faster reading shortens the delay. But procurement cannot judge AI impact, and forwarding still depends on someone recognizing an incident.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the fix will come as a vendor update. But wrong notices may already be reaching households; a release-cycle request delays triage of harm happening now.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because vendors should test releases. But no contract ends model flaws; this warning arrived and failed only because nobody who could act read it.

tips: Eliminate: C files a live harm as a routine change for later, and D asks for flawless releases instead of fixing how warnings are handled.
Final two: A beats B because incident intake brings named triage by impact; a faster inbox check still depends on procurement spotting the risk.
Exam cue: vendor notices, complaints and red-team findings are AI incident detection channels; check that they reach triage.

questions.question: A Czech poison-information center rates AI incidents by users affected and downtime, so a chatbot telling 12 callers a cleaning-product mix was safe was rated low. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Raise this incident to high and keep the current rating scale
options.B: Rate AI incidents by how many model outputs were affected
options.C: Add severity of harm to people to the AI incident rating scale
options.D: Have the IS auditor rate the severity of each AI incident

questions.key_concept: AI incident severity must weigh harm to people, not just user counts or downtime; a scale without it misrates harmful errors.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the rating scale measures, and whether a single serious harm could ever score high.
questions.correct_explanation: Wrongly telling 12 callers that a chemical mix was safe could injure them, yet a scale built on user counts and downtime rates it low. The scale itself is the gap: AI incidents must be triaged by the severity of harm to people as well as by scale and business impact. Re-rating this incident fixes one case, but the next harmful answer with few users or no downtime would be misrated again.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because this incident is clearly underrated. But fixing one rating leaves the scale that misrated it in place for the next incident.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it measures spread. But output counts are another volume measure; they still miss how badly each person could be harmed.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the IS auditor is objective. But rating incidents is the incident team's operating task; the IS auditor assesses the method.

tips: Eliminate: B swaps one volume measure for another, and D gives the IS auditor an operating task that belongs to the incident team.
Final two: C beats A because the scale caused the misrating; re-rating one incident leaves the next one exposed.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. Kill switch readiness
questions.question: An Egyptian irrigation authority's canal-gate model has a tested kill switch to its previous version, its only fallback, which reads the same sensor feeds. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Test the kill switch each month as well as before go-live
options.B: Obtain a vendor attestation that both versions tolerate feed faults
options.C: Rely on the previous model version as the fallback
options.D: Prepare and rehearse a manual way to operate the gates

questions.key_concept: Disengagement needs a rehearsed fallback that does not depend on the model or its feeds; an older version on the same inputs can fail alike.
questions.pre_read: Ask what takes over when the model is switched off, and whether it shares the model's weak points.
questions.correct_explanation: The kill switch hands the gates to the previous version, which reads the same sensor feeds, so a feed fault or a flaw both versions share would leave no safe way to run the gates. A rehearsed manual procedure gives a fallback that does not depend on any model, which makes disengagement a real option. Monthly kill-switch tests keep the handover working, but add nothing that works when both versions fail.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because tested switches are reliable. But a switch that hands control to a version on the same feeds still leaves no fallback if both fail.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a vendor attestation sounds like assurance. But it is a claim, not a fallback; if the shared feeds fail, nothing safe takes over the gates.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because an earlier version is a known state. But it reads the same feeds, so one feed fault or shared flaw stops both; a manual fallback does not.

tips: Eliminate: A keeps testing a switch without asking what takes over, and B relies on a vendor's claim instead of a working fallback.
Final two: D beats C because the previous version shares the same feeds and may fail with them; only a manual fallback works when the models cannot be trusted.
Exam cue: disengaging an AI system needs a rehearsed fallback for its work that does not depend on the same model or feeds.

questions.question: A Malawian tobacco auction rolled back its bale-grading model after two days of wrong grades that set growers' pay; grading is now normal, but those payments stand uncorrected. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Close the incident, since grading has now returned to normal
options.B: Use decision logs to find and regrade the affected bales
options.C: Retrain the model on the affected bales' corrected grades
options.D: Start root cause analysis on the faulty model version

questions.key_concept: Containment is not the end: decision logs identify the people affected during the faulty period so their harm can be remedied.
questions.pre_read: Ask who was affected before the rollback, and how the auction would find them.
questions.correct_explanation: Rolling back stopped new wrong grades, but bales graded during those two days still carry wrong grades, and growers may already have been paid on them. The decision logs show which bales the faulty version graded, so they can be regraded and growers' payments corrected. Root cause analysis must follow, but it fixes the model for the future; it does nothing for growers already harmed by wrong grades.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because ordinary incidents can close once service is confirmed. But growers already paid on wrong grades are unremedied; finding and correcting them comes before closure.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it uses corrected data. But it is an untested change made before the cause is known, and it does not fix grades already issued.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because root cause prevents recurrence. But it serves future sales; growers already harmed need their grades corrected first.

tips: Eliminate: A treats rollback as the end of the incident, and C makes an untested change before the cause is known.
Final two: B beats D because bales already carry wrong grades that growers are paid on; finding and remedying them comes before diagnosing the model.
Exam cue: after containment, use decision logs to identify the people affected and remedy their harm.

questions.question: A Uruguayan wool mill's output-forecast model began over-forecasting when a new truck scale arrived, whose readings for similar loads are 2.2 times the old scale's. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Correct the truck scale feed's units through change control
options.B: Retrain the model on recent data including the truck scale readings
options.C: Roll back to the previous model version until it is fixed
options.D: Widen the forecast alert threshold to absorb the larger readings

questions.key_concept: Root cause analysis for AI traces failures across data, model, prompt and integration layers; fix the layer that failed, through change control.
questions.pre_read: Ask what changed in the inputs when the problem began, before deciding what to fix.
questions.correct_explanation: A jump of about 2.2 times for similar loads is the pounds-to-kilograms ratio, so the cause sits in the integration layer: the new scale's feed sends the wrong units. The model is behaving as designed on wrong inputs, so the fix belongs in the feed through change control. Rolling back to an earlier model changes nothing, since that version would receive the same inflated weights; retraining would teach the model to treat pounds as normal.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because retraining adapts the model. But it would learn from mislabeled units, hiding the fault and breaking forecasts again once the feed is fixed.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because rollback is a standard containment step. But the model did not change; an older version fed the same wrong units fails the same way.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the larger readings now trip forecast alerts. But widening the threshold hides a real error from monitoring instead of correcting it.

tips: Eliminate: B teaches the model to accept wrong units, and D widens the alert threshold, so monitoring stops flagging a real input fault.
Final two: A beats C because the cause is in the feed; rolling back a model that did not change leaves the wrong units flowing.
Exam cue: trace an AI failure across layers (data, model, prompt, integration) before choosing a fix; the model is not always the cause.

questions.subtopic: 2G AI incident response. Closing problem records
questions.question: A Guyanese water utility's voice bot failed Creolese-speaking callers three times as often as others; a retrained version passed release tests, and the problem record was closed. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Keep the record closed, since the retrained version passed its tests
options.B: Add a notice that the bot may misunderstand some ways of speaking
options.C: Reopen the record until production results show the gap has closed
options.D: Have the IS auditor retest the retrained voice bot before closing

questions.key_concept: AI problem records close only when production evidence shows the fix removed the harm, not when a retrained version passes release tests.
questions.pre_read: Ask what evidence shows callers are now understood, and when it was gathered.
questions.correct_explanation: A problem record closes when the cause is removed and the fix is shown to work. Release tests show the retrained version met its criteria before go-live, not that Creolese-speaking callers now get through. Keeping the record open until production results by language show the gap has closed gives that proof. Closing on release tests alone could leave the gap in place, unseen.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because tests passed. But release tests show the version met its criteria; only production results show Creolese-speaking callers now get through.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it warns callers. But a notice treats the symptom; Creolese speakers would still be failed by the bot.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the IS auditor is independent. But verifying a fix is management's task; the IS auditor assesses whether it was done.

tips: Eliminate: B adds a notice while callers are still failed, and D gives the IS auditor verification work that management owns.
Final two: C beats A because release tests do not prove the harm stopped; production results by group show whether the fix worked.
Exam cue: close an AI problem record only when evidence from production shows the fix worked for the people affected.
